To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the protease inhibitors are not the only drugs to which the HIV-1 virus can develop resistance, (2) that resistance to the non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) efavirenz is also associated with the emergence of protease and integrase mutations, and that (3) that resistance to protease inhibitors is associated with the selection of mutations in the Gag and gp41 regions.

The use of the protease inhibitor (PI) lopinavir (LPV) as part of antiretroviral therapy (ART) is a major cause of the selection of mutations that are associated with resistance to PI and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) in HIV-1 infected individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new strategies to improve our understanding and treatment of viral infections, in particular HIV-1, and to develop new drugs for the treatment of viral diseases.
the identification of novel mechanisms of resistance in HIV-1 protease inhibitors.
the study of the resistance to the protease inhibitors in the treatment of HIV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of protease inhibitors in the context of virological failure is a risk factor for the selection of non-described resistance mutations.
the use of a combination of protease inhibitors and nucleoside analogues is the best option for the control of HIV infection.
protease inhibitors have a high genetic barrier to resistance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the resistance mutations to protease inhibitors in virological failures to protease inhibitors are not only the mutations described in the Stanford database, but also the non-described mutations.
the protease, Gp41 and Gag regions have a role in the resistance of protease inhibitor (PI) therapy in patients with virological failure (VF).
HIV-1 protease inhibitors (PIs) are still a very useful class of anti-retroviral drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the protease inhibitor class of antiretrovirals is still very important for treating HIV infection, even in the face of drug resistance.
we have shown that the protease inhibitors are not as effective in preventing HIV transmission as previously thought.
the use of protease inhibitors in HIV-1 infected patients can lead to the selection of non-described mutations in the Gag, Gp41 and PR genes, which could be responsible for the virological failure.
